title: The Whale

jokes.text: That Swayze sure can dance dirty.
jokes.setup: Andy is on a sailing trip, video-calling the office. He mentions he's seen Dirty Dancing 10 times and it breaks his heart every time.
jokes.punchline: His earnest, deeply sincere summary: 'That Swayze sure can dance dirty' — a man utterly unashamed of his emotional investment in a romantic dance film.
jokes.explanation: Works because it's so perfectly Andy — sincere, unguarded, and weirdly earnest. The economy is excellent; the whole joke is just that one sentence delivered with total conviction. Character integration is high because this is precisely the kind of thing Andy Bernard would say without irony.

jokes.text: You want to worry about a part of my body, worry about my eyes. They're like two flaming meatballs in my skull.
jokes.setup: Someone (likely Darryl via Skype) expresses concern about Andy not having sunblock.
jokes.punchline: Andy deflects to his eyes, describing them with the gloriously specific image of 'two flaming meatballs in my skull.'
jokes.explanation: The image of 'two flaming meatballs in my skull' is genuinely original and surprising — it's not a phrase anyone has heard before, it's grotesquely specific, and it comes from a place of total sincerity. High quotability because the phrase is so vivid and weird. This is above-average joke writing.

jokes.text: I was kind of sad at first, but then I remembered that Bob Marley song — No, Woman. No Cry.
jokes.setup: Darryl explains in a talking head that Andy took his brother sailing but not him.
jokes.punchline: He appears to be consoling himself with the uplifting spirit of the song, but the title itself — 'No Woman No Cry' — is being deployed as literal logic: no woman (Erin) came, so no crying necessary.
jokes.explanation: Smart structure: it seems like a feel-good rationalization, but the punchline is the song title itself reframed as pragmatic logic. The setup is perfectly calibrated for the payoff. Economy is excellent — the joke is entirely contained in one sentence. Good misdirection.

jokes.text: Check this out. Keeps my hair out of my stare, also helps me combat the glare bear. That's what I call the sun now.
jokes.setup: Andy is showing the camera something on his head (presumably underwear).
jokes.punchline: The rhyming scheme ('stare'/'glare bear') is absurd enough, but the kicker is 'That's what I call the sun now' — a completely unnecessary, self-satisfied rebranding of a celestial body.
jokes.explanation: The kicker 'That's what I call the sun now' is the best part — the casual ownership of renaming the sun is a perfect Andy move. The rhyming feels a bit try-hard but the closing line rescues it. Good character integration: only Andy would feel the need to announce a personal rebrand of the sun.

jokes.text: Andy, it's Darryl. Take your drawers off your head.
jokes.setup: Andy has been cheerfully showing off his makeshift sun-visor — which is, apparently, a pair of underwear on his head.
jokes.punchline: Darryl's flat, long-suffering delivery: 'Take your drawers off your head.' The visual is confirmed by the line.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — 'Take your drawers off your head' is seven words that do enormous work. Darryl as the deadpan straight man to Andy's chaos is well-established, and this is a clean execution of that dynamic. The visual gag (underwear on head) amplifies it.

jokes.text: Andy spills his drinking water and then confidently introduces his desalinator, which immediately sprays him in the face.
jokes.setup: Andy spills his freshwater and reassures everyone he has a cool desalinator device to replace it.
jokes.punchline: He demonstrates it and it immediately malfunctions and sprays him: 'Ow!'
jokes.explanation: Classic slapstick escalation — boast followed immediately by failure. The structure is competent and the timing is presumably good, but it's a fairly standard 'guy demonstrates thing, thing breaks' beat. Gets a solid laugh but not memorable.

jokes.text: I will leave you with this, the image of a man and his boat. Burn this into your brains.
jokes.setup: Andy is signing off from the Skype call, apparently feeling very romantic and cinematic about his sailing adventure.
jokes.punchline: He dramatically stages a farewell image — and then immediately falls off the boat.
jokes.explanation: The pomposity of 'burn this into your brains' followed by immediate pratfall is a satisfying escalation/subversion combo. Andy's self-mythologizing is perfectly in character. The physical payoff (falling off the boat) elevates what could have been a simple slapstick moment.

jokes.text: Well, hi, there, David Wallace. Why would you ever call me when the manager's out of town?
jokes.setup: David Wallace calls the office. The implication is that Dwight answers because Andy is gone.
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately frames the call as an obvious no-brainer — of course Wallace would call HIM, the obvious choice, when the manager is away.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's manic self-importance is perfectly captured — he immediately reframes the call as validation of his natural supremacy. Strong character integration because this is exactly how Dwight thinks. The rhetorical question directed at David is a nice touch.

jokes.text: And you didn't call Jim. That seems significant.
jokes.setup: David Wallace calls with big news. Jim walks in and Dwight has to acknowledge him.
jokes.punchline: Dwight, instead of just being professional, can't resist pointing out to David — pointedly, in front of Jim — that Jim wasn't called first. 'That seems significant.'
jokes.explanation: The barely-contained triumph in 'That seems significant' is excellent Dwight character work. He can't just let it go — he has to underline it. Economy is strong: four words do exactly as much as they need to. The passive-aggressive framing as an 'observation' rather than a gloat is the craft.

jokes.text: The White Pages. Do you want it? No. Do you use it? No. Does it inexplicably show up on your doorstep three times a year? Yes, yes, and yes.
jokes.setup: Wallace announces that the Scranton White Pages dropped their supplier and are looking to switch.
jokes.punchline: Wallace delivers a rapid-fire rhetorical breakdown of everyone's actual relationship with the White Pages, landing on the absurd 'inexplicably shows up three times a year' as the defining truth.
jokes.explanation: Sharp observational comedy with excellent rhythmic structure — the three-part rhetorical question builds perfectly. 'Inexplicably shows up three times a year' captures a universal truth about the White Pages in a very specific and funny way. The structure is almost stand-up quality, which is appropriate for Wallace's character.

jokes.text: Look at all that sweet blubber.
jokes.setup: Wallace has just called the White Pages 'the white whale' of the paper industry.
jokes.punchline: Dwight, staring at the phone/the concept, says 'Look at all that sweet blubber' — extending the whale metaphor with carnivorous delight.
jokes.explanation: Five words of perfect Dwight. The predatory joy, the literal-minded extension of a metaphor, the hunter's eye for a prize — all of it is Dwight in miniature. Economy score is near-perfect. Only slightly dinged because the joke doesn't quite rise to the level of genuine surprise.

jokes.text: Ha! Yeah! Whoo! Eat it, Jim! Eat it, Phyllis! Eat--
jokes.setup: Wallace tells Dwight he's the top salesman and needs to run point on this account. Dwight puts David on hold.
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately erupts in a victory celebration, naming colleagues one by one to eat it.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of calling out Jim AND Phyllis by name is the key — Phyllis is a lovely absurd choice. Dwight's competitive joy at being recognized is entirely in character. The truncation ('Eat--') implies he went on even longer, which is a smart structural choice.

jokes.text: Where's Stanley? Will you run to the bathroom and tell him to eat it? Of course.
jokes.setup: Dwight is celebrating being chosen as top salesman. Stanley is apparently not in the room.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's need to inform Stanley specifically — in the bathroom — that he should 'eat it,' and someone (likely Erin) agrees to do this without question.
jokes.explanation: This is the escalation that makes joke 13 much funnier in retrospect. The image of someone running to a bathroom to relay 'eat it' from Dwight is absurd and perfect. The immediate 'of course' acceptance from whoever agrees to go makes it even better — everyone just plays along with Dwight's insanity. Strong character work and escalation.

jokes.text: Gina Rogers at Apex Technology said you called her 'gy-na' for your entire meeting.
jokes.setup: Jim says Dwight can't go to the meeting because he has a problem with women.
jokes.punchline: Jim provides a specific, mortifying example: Dwight mispronounced a client's name 'Gina' as 'Gy-na' — which sounds like a slur for female anatomy — for the entire meeting.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent cringe comedy — specific, character-rooted, and with an implied horror that extends well beyond what's said. The detail that she corrected him five times and he persisted is what elevates it. Character integration is high because only Dwight's specific brand of obliviousness could produce this situation.

jokes.text: Gy-na said that?
jokes.setup: Jim has just explained that 'Gina' Rogers complained about Dwight mispronouncing her name as 'Gy-na.'
jokes.punchline: Dwight's response refers to her as 'Gy-na' again — proving he still doesn't get it, or genuinely doesn't understand the problem.
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the episode. Three words that are structurally perfect: the immediate callback, the total lack of self-awareness, and the devastating implication that Dwight will never stop calling her that. Economy is essentially perfect — every word works. Character integration is as high as it gets: this joke is impossible for any character other than Dwight. The structure of setup (Jim's story) and payoff (Dwight's response) is masterfully efficient. Comparable in craft to the vasectomy anchor example — it doesn't have that joke's escalation, but the economy and character specificity are at that level.

jokes.text: Pizza Friday could come back. Hey, remember that week in the '90s when we got bagels? I miss Clinton.
jokes.setup: Pam lists the potential benefits of landing the White Pages account: raises, bonuses, and 'Pizza Friday could come back.'
jokes.punchline: Someone (likely Kevin) immediately fondly recalls 'that week in the '90s when we got bagels,' and another voice adds 'I miss Clinton' — a non-sequitur that conflates political nostalgia with bagel nostalgia.
jokes.explanation: 'I miss Clinton' as a punchline to a bagel conversation is genuinely inspired — it implies that the bagels were so good, and so singular, that they're associated with an entire presidential era. The escalation from Pizza Friday to 'that week in the '90s' to full Clinton-era nostalgia is a beautifully compressed escalation. Highly quotable and original.

jokes.text: I have this conference call today with this company in Philly that I'm helping start — first board meeting, also the first time I've ever been excited about work, so that feels... wrong.
jokes.setup: Jim says he can't go to the White Pages meeting because he has a thing — the Philly startup board meeting.
jokes.punchline: He undercuts his own excitement with 'the first time I've ever been excited about work, so that feels... wrong' — a self-aware acknowledgment of his famously low-enthusiasm attitude toward Dunder Mifflin.
jokes.explanation: Good self-aware character work that also foreshadows the Jim/Philly subplot. The 'that feels... wrong' beat works as both a joke and as character development for season 9 Jim. Character integration is high because this is specifically about Jim's long relationship with workplace ennui.

jokes.text: Okay, calm down. It's just me, not Tom Selleck.
jokes.setup: The Movember mustache reveal — Toby has organized everyone to grow mustaches for charity.
jokes.punchline: Toby, with his characteristic lack of self-awareness, tells people to 'calm down' about his mustache and compares himself to Tom Selleck.
jokes.explanation: Toby comparing himself to Tom Selleck is funny because it's so perfectly Toby — the sad delusion of grandeur from the office's most put-upon character. The 'calm down' is the right setup for the payoff. Solid character comedy.

jokes.text: I hope you like being turned on all the time. Damn! It just keeps on coming, huh?
jokes.setup: The Movember mustache reveal. The camera pans across the mustachioed office men.
jokes.punchline: Meredith (most likely) says 'I hope you like being turned on all the time' and Kevin adds 'Damn! It just keeps on coming, huh?' — both delivered with varying degrees of sincerity and obliviousness.
jokes.explanation: Functional comedy — the mustache reveal joke is competent but predictable. 'Turned on all the time' is the obvious joke to make about a room full of mustachioed men, and Kevin's addendum is fine but not clever. Gets the job done without distinction.

jokes.text: I have very fertile hair glands.
jokes.setup: The Movember mustache segment. Dwight presumably has grown an impressive mustache.
jokes.punchline: Dwight explains his mustache growth in a talking head with the medically nonsensical phrase 'very fertile hair glands.'
jokes.explanation: 'Fertile hair glands' is a perfectly Dwight phrase — pseudo-scientific, slightly disturbing, and delivered with total conviction. The word 'fertile' applied to hair glands has a specific wrongness that is very funny. Strong economy and character integration.

jokes.text: We have the dopest time back in the annex. We even go to lunch, pick up babes. Smile if you love men's prostates.
jokes.setup: Ryan talking head about Movember in the annex. He's describing the social aspects of growing mustaches for charity.
jokes.punchline: 'Smile if you love men's prostates' — Ryan using the charity's medical cause as an extremely awkward pickup line.
jokes.explanation: Ryan's delusional hipster energy is well-captured here. 'Smile if you love men's prostates' is absurd and specific enough to be funny — it's the kind of thing only Ryan would consider a charming approach. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Spring cleaning? More like fall cleaning.
jokes.setup: Oscar apparently comments on what Pam or Angela is doing, calling it 'spring cleaning.'
jokes.punchline: The correction: 'More like fall cleaning.' A weak joke that's barely a joke — it's November, so it's fall.
jokes.explanation: This is a very weak joke — it's essentially just a calendar correction dressed up as wit. 'More like fall cleaning' is the kind of line that gets a polite smile at best. No originality, no character specificity, no surprise. The setup and punchline are the same observation said two ways.

jokes.text: I think the Senator is having an affair.
jokes.setup: Angela drops this bombshell completely out of nowhere during what appears to be a mundane conversation.
jokes.punchline: The abrupt, non-sequitur delivery of a devastating personal revelation as if it's a casual observation.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the delivery mode — Angela drops 'I think the Senator is having an affair' with the same energy as a mundane workplace observation. The contrast between the weight of the statement and the flat affect creates the joke. Good economy and structure.

jokes.text: I literally have nightmares in which what just happened happens.
jokes.setup: Angela has just told Oscar she thinks the Senator is having an affair. Oscar, who is secretly having an affair with the Senator, has to respond.
jokes.punchline: Oscar's talking-head confession that this is literally his recurring nightmare — perfectly capturing his guilty panic while being funny through the tortured grammar.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) the meta-humor of a nightmare about exactly this situation, (2) the tortured syntax 'nightmares in which what just happened happens' which is itself funny, (3) the dramatic irony for viewers who know Oscar IS the affair. The character integration is about as high as it gets — this joke is only possible because of Oscar's specific secret. A strong 8+ candidate.

jokes.text: And then I make Angela's husband spoon me back to bed.
jokes.setup: Oscar has just said he has nightmares about Angela suspecting the affair. He describes waking up in a sweat.
jokes.punchline: The punchline reveals that his comfort mechanism is having Angela's husband — the man he's having an affair with — spoon him back to sleep.
jokes.explanation: This is the strongest joke in the episode. It works on every level: (1) The dark irony of being comforted FROM the nightmare of discovery BY the person who would cause the discovery is perfectly constructed. (2) The word 'spoon' does tremendous work — specific, domestic, and somehow more transgressive than anything more explicit. (3) It's only possible for Oscar in this specific situation. (4) It escalates joke 26 to a devastating degree. This is comparable to the vasectomy anchor — it has genuine surprise, escalation, and character specificity all working together. The best joke of the episode.

jokes.text: Angela, Blake's also a guy's name, so he may be spending his afternoons with a guy named Blake. So nothing to worry about.
jokes.setup: Angela is worried because the Senator goes to hot yoga with someone named Blake and never misses it.
jokes.punchline: Oscar reassures her that 'Blake is also a guy's name' — technically true, and also a massive red flag that Oscar is desperately trying to neutralize while himself knowing the truth.
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is rich here — Oscar's 'reassurance' is also a kind of confession for those paying attention. The comedy of a guilty party reassuring the aggrieved party is classic but well-executed. The 'So nothing to worry about' closer is perfectly hollow and desperate.

jokes.text: Huh. Blake. Who is Blake? I don't know. I just never heard about the Senator and yoga from you.
jokes.setup: Oscar overreacted slightly to the name 'Blake' and is now walking it back in conversation with Pam.
jokes.punchline: The visible awkwardness of Oscar trying to un-ring a bell — the flailing explanation 'I just never heard about the Senator and yoga from you' is the comedy of someone digging themselves in deeper.
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy but less precise than the preceding Oscar jokes. The back-pedaling is recognizable and relatable but the specific lines aren't especially crafted. Serves the plot more than the comedy.

jokes.text: We need to go and check this out. — Angela, I'll go with you.
jokes.setup: Angela decides she needs to investigate whether the Senator is having an affair at the yoga studio.
jokes.punchline: Oscar immediately volunteers to come — because he knows exactly what they'll find, and yet he can't stop himself, presumably to manage the situation.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the dramatic irony — Oscar volunteering to chaperone the discovery of his own affair. It's a classic farce structure executed in The Office's low-key style. Good character integration, though the joke relies heavily on audience foreknowledge.

jokes.text: May I please speak to your boss? — No, she is the boss. — I am?
jokes.setup: The team is role-playing a sales meeting to prepare Dwight for meeting a female client. Pam plays the receptionist, Nellie plays the buyer.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's first move is to ask for the boss, and when told the woman IS the boss, he immediately turns to Nellie and says 'I am?' — completely breaking the roleplay because he can't even simulate the concept.
jokes.explanation: The 'I am?' is the perfect punchline — it reveals that Dwight's sexism is so embedded that he can't even play-act past it. Breaking the fourth wall of the roleplay by seeking confirmation from the woman playing the boss is structurally elegant. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Okay, this isn't working for me, 'cause no one would ever believe that she would be a boss. — He's absolutely right. I'm really struggling here.
jokes.setup: Dwight has already failed the roleplay by asking for the boss despite being told Pam IS the boss.
jokes.punchline: Dwight says the quiet part loud — 'no one would ever believe she'd be a boss' — and Pam, hilariously, agrees with him in the context of the roleplay.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Pam's agreement — she's so committed to helping that she validates Dwight's sexism within the frame of the exercise, which is a small but funny bit of character self-deprecation from Pam. Dwight's candor is on-brand.

jokes.text: I never sit down during sales meetings. I want to appear aggressive, imposing. I am going to sell to you in 12 minutes. No, actually, she'd like to take her time. I will tell her what her needs are and then fill them. This is gonna work out best for you if you just relax and do nothing. And once I'm finished, it's over.
jokes.setup: The roleplay continues. Nellie tries to redirect Dwight toward listening and respecting the client's needs.
jokes.punchline: Dwight bulldozes through every correction with an increasingly rape-metaphor-adjacent sales pitch, culminating in 'once I'm finished, it's over.'
jokes.explanation: This is a masterfully escalating cringe sequence. Each of Dwight's lines builds on the previous one to create an increasingly horrifying portrait of his sales approach. 'I will tell her what her needs are and then fill them' and 'once I'm finished, it's over' are the peak — the double entendre is fully earned by the escalation. Strong structure and character integration.

jokes.text: I thought it went great. / One. Have you ever killed a woman? How many women have you killed? Please, sir, will you not kill me?
jokes.setup: The roleplay has just concluded in a horror show. The group asks for feedback.
jokes.punchline: Dwight thinks it went great. Nellie has written down three questions: escalating from 'have you ever killed a woman' to the terrified plea 'please, sir, will you not kill me?'
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'have you ever killed a woman' to a direct plea 'please sir will you not kill me' is a beautifully compressed joke. Nellie's feedback framed as murder-related questions perfectly summarizes how threatening Dwight's approach felt. The terror escalation in three beats is well-structured. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: The board call is spooky-sexy. 'I think there's been a mistake. We're trying to reach Jim Halpert, not Batman.'
jokes.setup: Jim is on his first board call with the Philly startup. He's trying to find a good spot to take the call and the audio quality is terrible and dramatic.
jokes.punchline: The voice on the call is described as 'spooky-sexy,' and then the team says they're 'trying to reach Jim Halpert, not Batman' — suggesting his audio sounds like a superhero.
jokes.explanation: 'Trying to reach Jim Halpert, not Batman' is a clean, quotable joke. The 'spooky-sexy' descriptor is also a nice absurdist touch. Good economy. The Jim-in-over-his-head subplot is well-served by this comedic beat.

jokes.text: Listening happens in the ear and in the brain. I mean, some organisms have external hairs that vibrate to indicate auditory stimulation, but unfortunately, our external hairs don't vibrate at all.
jokes.setup: Pam tells Dwight he has to SHOW them he's listening. He says that's impossible.
jokes.punchline: Dwight delivers a pseudo-scientific lecture on the biology of listening, referencing organisms with vibrating external hairs.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dwight: deflect a simple human request with arcane pseudo-scientific knowledge. The specificity of 'external hairs that vibrate to indicate auditory stimulation' is exactly the kind of detail that makes Dwight jokes work. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight's nodding face — 'I can't. I just can't carry on with that face. He looks like he's laboring over a stool, having just eaten human flesh.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has been instructed to show he's listening by smiling and nodding. He attempts this.
jokes.punchline: Nellie can't continue the roleplay because Dwight's 'listening face' looks like 'he's laboring over a stool, having just eaten human flesh.'
jokes.explanation: Nellie's description is extraordinary: 'laboring over a stool, having just eaten human flesh.' The two-part image — constipation PLUS cannibalism — is so specifically wrong and funny that it elevates a standard 'character has a bad face' joke into something memorable. High originality for the specific phrasing. This is Nellie at her best as a comedic foil.

jokes.text: Oh, are those your kids? They're so cute. They could be models. / Thank you. I carried each one of them for nine months inside of my torso and then pushed them out of my vagina.
jokes.setup: Jim demonstrates how to be personable with a female client by complimenting her children. Dwight plays the female client.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's response as 'the woman' is to provide a graphic, clinical birth narrative — 'nine months inside of my torso and then pushed them out of my vagina' — as a natural conversational response to a compliment.
jokes.explanation: Dwight playing 'the woman' and immediately turning a pleasant compliment into a clinical gynecological report is very funny — it shows exactly why Dwight cannot relate to women even when trying his hardest. The word 'torso' is a specifically funny anatomical misdirection before 'vagina.' Works well.

jokes.text: Ten years ago, I didn't care if Dwight got married or died a beet-farming bachelor. But having kids makes you so soft. I used to watch Pulp Fiction and laugh, and now I'm like, 'that poor gimp is somebody's child.'
jokes.setup: Jim talking head about why he's invested in helping Dwight succeed with this female client.
jokes.punchline: 'I used to watch Pulp Fiction and laugh, and now I'm like, that poor gimp is somebody's child.' The Pulp Fiction gimp as an object of parental sympathy is the absurdist punchline.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The setup (parenthood makes you soft) is relatable, but the punchline — applying parental sympathy to the Pulp Fiction gimp specifically — is a genuinely unexpected and perfect comedic leap. 'That poor gimp is somebody's child' is an extraordinary sentence. The character integration is excellent: Jim as a new father who talks about pop culture is exactly right. Highly quotable and original.

jokes.text: I have no problem with women. It's businesswomen and their power suits and their shoulder pads. Don't lie about your shoulders.
jokes.setup: Dwight insists he doesn't have a problem with women in response to Pam's coaching.
jokes.punchline: 'Don't lie about your shoulders' — Dwight's specific grievance with shoulder pads as a form of deception.
jokes.explanation: 'Don't lie about your shoulders' is a great Dwight line — it takes a completely mundane fashion observation and frames it as a moral failing. The specificity of shoulder pads as Dwight's particular grievance against businesswomen is funny and character-perfect. Strong economy.

jokes.text: I had a barber once who used to comb my hair gently. / Okay, so when you're selling to this woman, just imagine she's that nice, reasonable barber.
jokes.setup: Pam asks Dwight to name a nice, reasonable person from his experience. A long pause follows.
jokes.punchline: The best Dwight can do is a barber who 'combed his hair gently' — the barest minimum of human kindness — and Pam, committed to making this work, adopts it as the strategy.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'combed my hair gently' as the ceiling of Dwight's positive human experiences is both funny and a little sad. Pam adopting it wholesale — 'okay, just imagine she's that nice, reasonable barber' — is a great straight-man commitment. Strong character integration for Dwight.

jokes.text: He used to fight dogs. / Like, he used to make dogs fight, or he actually fought dogs? / Little of this, little of that.
jokes.setup: Dwight has just described the barber as a nice, reasonable person. Then he adds a postscript.
jokes.punchline: The barber fought dogs (both as organizer and participant, it's implied), and Dwight presents this as a minor biographical footnote rather than a disqualifying character detail.
jokes.explanation: The callback structure is perfect: the barber was established as Dwight's beacon of human kindness, and then immediately revealed to be a dogfighter. Pam's clarifying question ('make dogs fight or actually fought dogs') is excellent straight-man work. 'Little of this, little of that' as Dwight's breezy answer is perfect economy — it implies both are true without committing to either. This is a very strong joke. Among the episode's best.

jokes.text: Which one is the instructor? — They're all fatties.
jokes.setup: Angela and Oscar are outside the yoga studio, looking for Blake.
jokes.punchline: Angela's assessment of the class as 'they're all fatties' — delivered as an observation, not an insult — is purely Angela.
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely in the character — 'fatties' is a perfectly Angela word, delivered with her characteristic pinched judgment. Strong character integration and economy, but the underlying joke (mean person says something mean) is not very original or crafted.

jokes.text: She's so stunningly tiny. She's like a petite double zero for sure, for sure.
jokes.setup: Blake turns out to be a very small woman — the yoga instructor.
jokes.punchline: Angela immediately pivots from suspicion to admiration, fixating on the instructor's tiny size with obvious competitive envy.
jokes.explanation: Angela's obsession with thinness and her immediate switch from jealousy to admiration is good character work. The 'double zero for sure, for sure' repetition captures her fixation well. Not a crafted joke so much as a strong character beat.

jokes.text: She's repositioning his hips for downward-facing dog. I've heard of this — dog style.
jokes.setup: Angela is watching the yoga instructor adjust a student's hips in a pose called 'downward-facing dog.'
jokes.punchline: Angela connects 'downward-facing dog' to 'dog style' — a conflation of the yoga pose with a sexual position — apparently not fully understanding the joke she's making.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Angela's apparent sincerity — she seems genuinely to be connecting 'dog' to 'dog style' as if this is useful yoga knowledge. The joke is enhanced by her character but the wordplay itself is fairly obvious. Functional.

jokes.text: Thumbelina has a boyfriend. And he has a ponytail? Ew. I'd like to see that run for office.
jokes.setup: The tiny yoga instructor (Blake) is shown with a boyfriend who has a ponytail.
jokes.punchline: Angela dismisses the boyfriend for his ponytail and then imagines him in politics — 'I'd like to see that run for office' — referencing her own husband the Senator's political image.
jokes.explanation: The political reference is a nice character-specific touch — Angela's frame of reference for 'acceptable man' is her senator husband. 'I'd like to see that run for office' is a good line with a layer of dramatic irony (we know her husband is the one with the secret). Good character integration.

jokes.text: Oscar, you were right. I had nothing to be worried about. Thank you. Let's go. — No, whoa, whoa. Shut up. Hold on.
jokes.setup: Angela sees Blake has a boyfriend and concludes her husband isn't having an affair. She's relieved and tries to leave.
jokes.punchline: Oscar stops her — because he knows they haven't seen the relevant information yet. Angela is about to leave the scene of her own husband's exposure while Oscar desperately tries to manage the situation.
jokes.explanation: The irony is rich: Oscar frantically trying to keep Angela from leaving so he can... what exactly? He can't help himself but also can't stop watching. The dramatic irony is well-executed cringe comedy. Character integration is excellent.

jokes.text: The Senator is seen through the yoga studio window clearly making an intimate phone call / interacting in a way that confirms the affair.
jokes.setup: Angela and Oscar watch through the yoga studio window. Angela was about to leave, relieved.
jokes.punchline: The Senator appears and his behavior makes the affair obvious — the audience and Oscar know, and now Angela sees it too. Oscar's 'This is fun. You know? This is fun.' is the absurdly inappropriate reaction beat.
jokes.explanation: Oscar's 'This is fun. You know? This is fun.' while watching his affair partner unknowingly reveal himself to his wife through a window is dark, specific, and brilliantly wrong. It captures Oscar's complicated position — guilty, excited, horrified — in an absurdly inappropriate register. Strong character integration and cringe comedy.

jokes.text: Do you mind telling me her name? — Uh, she'll be right in. / Just a little off the top and then a nice combing.
jokes.setup: Dwight is sitting in the waiting room before the White Pages meeting. He asks for the client's name and gets stonewalled.
jokes.punchline: Dwight, alone in the waiting room, tells himself 'just a little off the top and then a nice combing' — mentally rehearsing the barber visualization to stay calm.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the barber strategy lands well because it shows Dwight has actually absorbed the coaching — in his own bizarre way. Seeing him alone, quietly muttering 'just a little off the top and then a nice combing' to psych himself up is unexpectedly charming and funny. Strong callback structure.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. It's Jan. Oh, dear God in heaven.
jokes.setup: Dwight and Pam are waiting for the White Pages client. The client enters.
jokes.punchline: It's Jan — Pam's horrified reaction is the joke, plus the ten-second dramatic pause before her talking-head.
jokes.explanation: The reveal of Jan is a great structural surprise — the episode has been building up the mysterious female client and then pays off with a fan-favorite recurring character. Pam's 'Oh, dear God in heaven' perfectly captures the audience reaction. The moment is more structural than joke-crafted but lands very well.

jokes.text: Jan used to be one of my superiors, and she is one of the most erratic and terrifying people I have ever met. / You son of a bitch. You're firing me? / Jim and I are pretty sure she had an affair with her ex-assistant Hunter. He was 17. But she looks great. If she asks, will you tell her I said that?
jokes.setup: Pam's talking head about Jan, intercut with a flashback/memory of Jan's erratic behavior.
jokes.punchline: The escalating horror of Jan's description — erratic, terrifying, had an affair with a 17-year-old — is capped with Pam's completely sincere 'but she looks great' and the request to be passed a compliment.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'most erratic and terrifying person I've ever met / possible statutory affair' to 'but she looks great, tell her I said that' is a great tonal whiplash. Pam's earnest desire to pass on the compliment despite everything is very funny and very Pam. Good structure.

jokes.text: Jim and I are pretty sure she had an affair with her ex-assistant Hunter. He was 17. But she looks great. If she asks, will you tell her I said that?
jokes.setup: Pam is filling in background on Jan for the audience in a talking head.
jokes.punchline: Pam notes an alleged statutory affair, then pivots to 'but she looks great' — and the addition of 'if she asks, will you tell her I said that?' shows Pam is genuinely afraid of Jan while also genuinely complimenting her.
jokes.explanation: The three-beat structure is excellent: serious dark info (statutory affair) → genuine compliment (she looks great) → genuine fear (please tell her). The 'will you tell her I said that' directed at the camera crew/documentary team is a great mockumentary beat — Pam is trying to use the documentary to pass a compliment to someone she's afraid of. Strong character integration for Pam.

jokes.text: Forget everything we taught you.
jokes.setup: Jan has walked in. Pam knows all normal strategies are useless against Jan.
jokes.punchline: Pam tells Dwight to forget all the coaching — a complete reversal that acknowledges Jan exists outside normal social rules.
jokes.explanation: Four words that perfectly pay off a 7-minute comedic sequence. 'Forget everything we taught you' is great economy — it simultaneously acknowledges the futility of the prep and signals that Jan is uniquely dangerous. A strong callback punchline.

jokes.text: Hey, Jan! It's so great to see you!
jokes.setup: Pam has just said 'forget everything we taught you' — implying Dwight should improvise.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's improvisation is to open with maximum false enthusiasm — 'It's so great to see you!' said with the energy of a used-car dealer.
jokes.explanation: Functional joke — Dwight's overenthusiastic greeting after 'forget everything we taught you' is a decent beat, but it's not particularly crafted. The comedy is situational more than joke-level.

jokes.text: Your daughter could be a bubble-bath model. I could just bite her head off.
jokes.setup: Dwight is trying to compliment Jan's daughter, using the 'compliment children' technique Jim demonstrated.
jokes.punchline: He delivers a vaguely complimentary opener ('bubble-bath model') and then — unhinged — adds 'I could just bite her head off.'
jokes.explanation: The callback to the 'compliment children' strategy is perfect: Dwight tries to execute it but adds 'I could just bite her head off' — which is meant affectionately but sounds threatening. The contrast between the sweet intent and the violent phrasing is a great Dwight joke. Strong character integration and economy.

jokes.text: Molly! / David Wallace is in Vermont. / Oh, my God. Um, I talked to his assistant. And I guess it did get a little confusing 'cause you said not to tell anyone your name. And then also, these bluetooths are very hard to hear with. I know you love the way they look, but Tom never had us use them.
jokes.setup: Jan expected David Wallace to come to the meeting. She finds out it's Dwight instead.
jokes.punchline: The assistant Molly unravels a cascade of communication failures: she didn't catch the name, they use bluetooth earpieces Jan wears for fashion not function, and she drops the detail that 'Tom never had us use them.'
jokes.explanation: A layered cringe moment that efficiently establishes Jan's chaotic management style. The bluetooth detail ('you love the way they look') is a nice Jan-specific touch. Molly's bravery in mentioning Tom is funny. Competent ensemble cringe comedy.

jokes.text: Insightful, Pam.
jokes.setup: Pam has just stated that Jan isn't going to sell to them.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's dry 'Insightful, Pam' — delivered with barely disguised contempt for the obvious observation.
jokes.explanation: Two words of Dwight contempt delivered perfectly. The economy is essentially perfect but the joke itself isn't especially original — it's a standard 'sarcastic thanks for nothing' beat. Works in context.

jokes.text: Erin, did this call-- / Uh! Sorry. I just-- I saw your face. / Oh. I'm sorry. It's for the thing. / I know. That's great. It just -- it makes it look like there's an eyebrow in the middle of your face.
jokes.setup: Kevin approaches Erin about something (probably a Movember-related mustache discussion). She's startled by his face.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's Movember mustache apparently looks like 'an eyebrow in the middle of your face' — followed by a cascade of further descriptions.
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of Kevin's misplaced-eyebrow mustache is functional and the 'cyclops whose eye fell out' follow-up is a nice touch. But this is competent filler comedy rather than standout writing.

jokes.text: But, um, you look like a cyclops whose eye... fell out... which is great.
jokes.setup: Erin is describing the effect of Kevin's Movember mustache.
jokes.punchline: 'Which is great' — Erin's characteristic habit of ending potentially hurtful observations with hollow affirmations.
jokes.explanation: 'A cyclops whose eye fell out' is a genuinely funny image for Kevin's mustache — the addition of 'which is great' as Erin's reflexive positivity is strong character integration. The awkward trailing '...fell out...' adds a nice timing beat.

jokes.text: Astrid's song: ♪ Mommy, you're a princess / Mommy, you're a superstar / Mommy, you're the greatest / How can I ever fill your shoes? ♪
jokes.setup: Pam is keeping Jan occupied by asking about her daughter Astrid. Jan offers to show a slideshow.
jokes.punchline: The slideshow apparently includes a song — which is about how unattainably great Mommy is. 'How can I ever fill your shoes?' coming from a toddler is the absurd punchline.
jokes.explanation: The song is pitch-perfect Jan — she has apparently trained her toddler to sing her praises. 'How can I ever fill your shoes?' is both funny and deeply revealing about Jan's narcissism. The fact that a toddler is singing a song about the impossibility of living up to her mother is dark and very in-character for Jan.

jokes.text: Your voice is as lovely as ever. / Well, that was me too. / Oh, okay. It's just that's how Cece does it with the backwards Es.
jokes.setup: Pam compliments the singing, assuming it's Astrid. Jan reveals she sang too.
jokes.punchline: Pam, rather than recover gracefully, doubles down by explaining that the 'backwards Es' signature style is what Cece does — implying Cece's handwriting is what confused her, as if that's the real issue.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe moment — Pam's attempt to recover by blaming the confusion on backwards Es is a classic 'digging deeper' beat. The specificity of 'backwards Es' as the explanation is funny. Jan's cold 'Oh, okay' is strong.

jokes.text: Well, it's not really much of a comparison, is it? I mean, 'Cece' is two letters, and 'Astrid' is... I mean, there's even some adults who — who — who can't spell it.
jokes.setup: Jan is offended that Pam's daughter's name (Cece) was favorably compared to Astrid.
jokes.punchline: Jan gets into a petty name-complexity competition, noting that 'Cece is two letters' and that some adults can't spell 'Astrid' — implying Cece is too simple a name to compete.
jokes.explanation: Jan getting into a petty name-spelling competition is vintage Jan — the escalation to 'some adults can't spell it' as a flex is darkly funny because it's simultaneously a brag and an insult. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Can you spell it? Try to spell it, Pam. Um... A... X? I don't — you got me.
jokes.setup: Jan has been bragging about how uniquely difficult 'Astrid' is to spell.
jokes.punchline: She challenges Pam to spell it, and Pam's attempt bottoms out at 'A... X?' before giving up — accidentally validating Jan's point while also showing Pam's pleasant self-deprecation.
jokes.explanation: 'A... X? I don't — you got me.' is a great Pam moment — she gives up so easily and so cheerfully. The specific wrong letter (X) is perfectly chosen. Good cringe comedy with a strong Pam character beat.

jokes.text: Don't patronize me. / I'm so sorry. / I hate this. You're better. Okay, we should go now.
jokes.setup: Pam has apparently given Jan an easy out or a consoling response after the spelling challenge.
jokes.punchline: Jan's 'I hate this. You're better.' is a startling moment of self-awareness from Jan — she recognizes she's in a competition she started and is losing emotionally.
jokes.explanation: 'I hate this. You're better.' is an extraordinary Jan line — the sudden collapse from aggressive competition to frank admission is both funny and weirdly poignant. The economy is near-perfect: four words that reveal everything about Jan's competitive misery. This is Jan at her best as a character — the moments where the mask slips. High character integration, high quotability.

jokes.text: Oh, are you getting your jollies right now? Can't get enough of the show? Your jollies are all on fire.
jokes.setup: Oscar is watching the Senator through the yoga studio window with what appears to be fascination.
jokes.punchline: Angela accuses Oscar of enjoying watching her husband's suspected indiscretion — calling his 'jollies' 'all on fire' — completely unaware that Oscar's fascination is for entirely different reasons.
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is doing heavy lifting here — Angela accusing Oscar of enjoying the spectacle is correct, but for the wrong reasons. 'Your jollies are all on fire' is an unusual phrase that sounds vaguely Angela. Strong character integration given the secret Oscar is keeping.

jokes.text: It's Robert who's enjoying it. What? This could be the affair you're scared of. Politicians are wonderful liars. You never know who they really are. / But, uh, he's probably not gay. He's straight. He's straight, so...
jokes.setup: Oscar tries to redirect Angela's suspicions toward the Senator's male colleague 'Robert,' implying the Senator might be gay.
jokes.punchline: Having successfully planted the seed of doubt, Oscar then immediately backtracks: 'But, uh, he's probably not gay. He's straight. He's straight, so...' — a spectacular self-undermining.
jokes.explanation: Oscar talking himself into and immediately out of outing the Senator in real time is brilliant. The escalation — 'politicians are wonderful liars, you never know who they really are' (true! Oscar knows!) — followed by immediate reversal — 'but he's probably not gay, he's straight, he's straight' — shows Oscar's guilt and panic perfectly. The repetition of 'he's straight' is the tell. Excellent character integration and structure.

jokes.text: Jan: 'Could I get some more water?' — Receptionist: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Jan is meeting with Dwight and Pam. She asks for water.
jokes.punchline: The receptionist says 'No.' — flat, immediate, no explanation. Jan has apparently already made an enemy of her assistant in record time.
jokes.explanation: The single-word refusal — 'No.' — from the receptionist tells an entire story about Jan's management style without a word of exposition. Economy is almost perfect. The setup is elegant: a completely routine request for water, denied with no justification. Jan has already so thoroughly alienated her assistant that water is denied. Efficient and funny.

jokes.text: You thought I had no more cards left to play. Well, I've got one. Man-boy! The ace of babes.
jokes.setup: The meeting is at an impasse. Dwight excuses himself and returns with a secret weapon.
jokes.punchline: Dwight reveals his secret weapon is a young male employee (presumably Pete or Clark) and announces him as 'Man-boy! The ace of babes' — Dwight's understanding of female attraction delivered in his most theatrical voice.
jokes.explanation: 'Man-boy! The ace of babes.' is a great absurdist Dwight construction — the exclamation point energy, the card game metaphor applied to human attraction, and 'ace of babes' as a formal title. Dwight's strategy is to deploy an attractive young man as a sales tool, which is both offensive and weirdly strategic. High quotability — 'ace of babes' is a highly memorable phrase. Justifies strong scores.

jokes.text: Jan... You thought I had no more cards left to play. Well, I've got one. Man-boy! The ace of babes.
jokes.setup: The meeting with Jan is going poorly. Dwight excuses himself and returns with a surprise.
jokes.punchline: 'Man-boy! The ace of babes.' — Dwight dramatically reveals his secret weapon: a young, attractive man (presumably from the office). The nicknames are gloriously bizarre.
jokes.explanation: 'Man-boy! The ace of babes.' is one of the episode's best lines. The escalation from 'thought I had no cards' to this dramatic reveal, plus the completely original terminology ('man-boy,' 'ace of babes') is inventive and perfectly Dwight. This is the kind of phrase that sticks. High quotability, strong character integration — only Dwight would have a 'man-boy' in his sales arsenal.

jokes.text: Jan, may I introduce to you your own personal Dunder Mifflin liaison, devoted to servicing this account with total client satisfaction.
jokes.setup: Dwight introduces his secret weapon — a young, handsome man — to Jan as a business liaison.
jokes.punchline: The corporate-speak 'total client satisfaction' combined with the obviously non-business nature of the offer is Dwight's bizarrely honest scheme.
jokes.explanation: The corporate wrapper around a transparent ploy to pander to Jan's attraction to young men is amusing but less punchy than the 'ace of babes' setup. Functions as the explanation to the previous joke's punchline.

jokes.text: Nothing like, uh, your old assistant... Hunter. Was that his name?
jokes.setup: Dwight is selling the 'man-boy' to Jan by comparing him to her previous assistant.
jokes.punchline: Dwight brings up Hunter — the assistant Jan allegedly had an affair with when he was 17 — by name, with fake uncertainty ('Was that his name?'), as a sales pitch.
jokes.explanation: The fake casual 'Was that his name?' while clearly knowing exactly who Hunter is — and using this knowledge as a sales tactic — is deeply Dwight. The callback to the Hunter/Jan affair detail from Pam's talking head pays off in an unexpected and dark way. Dwight using statutory-adjacent history as a sales angle is wonderfully wrong and very specific to the character.

jokes.text: I-I-- / Hmm? / I don't recall. / And, yes, Molly is crap.
jokes.setup: Dwight has invoked Hunter. Jan is visibly flustered — 'I-I--' — then tries to deny remembering.
jokes.punchline: 'And, yes, Molly is crap.' — Jan pivots from the uncomfortable territory of Hunter to abruptly agreeing that her assistant is bad.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'I don't recall [Hunter]' to 'and yes, Molly is crap' is perfectly Jan — she changes the subject while also betraying something, and the casual 'crap' is a perfectly Jan word. The beat lands well.

jokes.text: He's been growing that mustache for weeks. Best he can do... so young.
jokes.setup: Dwight's 'man-boy' is revealed — apparently Ryan, with his Movember mustache.
jokes.punchline: Jan's appraising 'best he can do... so young' — with a pause — as she looks at the barely-there mustache is quietly devastating and very Jan.
jokes.explanation: The Movember callback lands beautifully: Ryan's weeks of mustache effort is appraised by Jan as 'best he can do... so young.' The 'so young' is the devastating kicker — Jan is more interested in youth than facial hair, and she's not embarrassed by this at all. The pause before 'so young' is important. Very strong Jan character integration and excellent economy.

jokes.text: Can you turn around for me, please? / Dwight, you can go.
jokes.setup: Jan is appraising Ryan. She asks him to turn around.
jokes.punchline: Having seen the full picture, Jan dismisses Dwight: 'You can go.' — the transaction is complete; Dwight is now superfluous.
jokes.explanation: The dismissal of Dwight the moment the man-boy has been appraised is a great beat — Jan's transactional approach to people, including her business contacts, is perfectly captured. The 'Dwight, you can go' feels like he's been literally replaced by Ryan.

jokes.text: Do you have a valid passport?
jokes.setup: Jan is interrogating Ryan after dismissing Dwight. The business pretense is dropping rapidly.
jokes.punchline: 'Do you have a valid passport?' — an utterly non-business question to ask a paper company liaison, but a completely Jan question to ask an attractive young man she's appraising.
jokes.explanation: Six words. 'Do you have a valid passport?' is a perfect closing joke for the Jan sequence. It tells an entire story: Jan is not buying paper, she is planning an international trip with this young man. The question is so specific (valid passport, not just 'passport'), so businesslike in phrasing, and so completely unrelated to paper sales that it earns maximum economy points. Character integration is near-perfect — this is only Jan. This is one of the episode's very best jokes.

jokes.text: Yeah, well, it's not just not ideal. I mean, with you there, I don't know how we're gonna do this.
jokes.setup: Jim has apologized for the chaos of his board call. Colin seemed understanding at first.
jokes.punchline: Colin walks it back: this isn't just 'not ideal' — Jim's physical absence is genuinely a problem. The Philly startup story takes a darker turn.
jokes.explanation: This is more plot than comedy — it's the moment where the Jim/Philly subplot gets serious. The cringe of Jim realizing this isn't going well is present but not played for laughs. Weak as a joke.

jokes.text: The Senator is seen outside on a phone call — 'Oh, oh!' — the reaction as it becomes clear something intimate is happening.
jokes.setup: The Senator has come outside while Angela and Oscar are watching. He gets on his phone.
jokes.punchline: Something about the call or his demeanor makes it evident to both watchers — the 'Oh, oh!' is the moment of realization, played as cringe comedy.
jokes.explanation: A strong visual cringe moment but light on crafted comedy — the impact is in the situation rather than in any specific joke. The wordless reaction is effective TV but harder to score as a joke.

jokes.text: Oh, hey, Molly. Um, you should just quit. / Yeah. Thanks. / Yeah. Okay. / Oh, and, uh, Molly... I know it can't be easy working for Jan. Good luck with your feelings.
jokes.setup: Dwight runs into Molly (Jan's assistant) on his way out.
jokes.punchline: 'Good luck with your feelings.' — Dwight's parting advice to Molly, which combines genuine empathy with total awkwardness.
jokes.explanation: 'Good luck with your feelings' is a great Dwight line. It's awkward, slightly clinical, but also genuinely compassionate in a Dwight way. The sequence leading up to it — casually telling her to quit, her resigned agreement, then the Dwight pivot to empathy — is perfectly structured. This is Dwight at his most weirdly touching and the comedy is in the gap between his affect and his actual warmth.

jokes.text: Oh, and, uh, Molly... I know it can't be easy working for Jan. Good luck with your feelings.
jokes.setup: Dwight has already told Molly to quit. He pauses as if he has more to say.
jokes.punchline: 'Good luck with your feelings' — as if working for Jan will inevitably produce unspecified feelings that require luck to navigate. The phrase is both oddly empathetic and completely bizarre.
jokes.explanation: 'Good luck with your feelings' is a standout Dwight line — it's empathetic in content but delivered as if feelings are a foreign country he's wishing her safe passage through. The phrase acknowledges emotional experience while keeping it at arm's length, which is the defining characteristic of Dwight's emotional intelligence. High quotability. Justifies 8+ for originality, character integration, and economy.

jokes.text: You should ask for her number. / Oh, I got her number. 415-YCL. / That's a license number? / That's all you need.
jokes.setup: Pam suggests Dwight ask Molly for her number, presumably because Pam thought they had a moment.
jokes.punchline: Dwight reveals he already got her number — but it's a license plate number (415-YCL), not a phone number. He's treating courtship like a surveillance operation.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent Dwight character comedy. The assumption that 'her number' means a license plate — and the confidence that 'that's all you need' — perfectly encapsulates Dwight's approach to both romance and information gathering. '415-YCL' being an actual specific number is a great detail. 'That's all you need' as a romantic philosophy is deeply Dwight. One of the episode's strongest jokes.

jokes.text: Because you are my friend and you are a woman... and women love gossip, it's like air to you people. Ugh, God.
jokes.setup: Pam asks why Dwight would tell her when he's 'curried favor' with Molly.
jokes.punchline: Dwight explains it's because Pam is a woman and 'women love gossip, it's like air to you people' — an absurd generalization delivered with total conviction and a weary 'Ugh, God' that suggests he finds it exhausting.
jokes.explanation: The 'Ugh, God' at the end — as if Dwight is exhausted by his own knowledge of women's gossip needs — is the key to this joke. The generalization is pure Dwight: stated as anthropological fact. Strong character integration.

tmdb_overview: The women of the office try to teach Dwight how to interact with female clients; Angela suspects the senator of cheating; Toby convinces some of the guys to grow mustaches.
